title: Key agreement from one-way functions
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[\(f(Y)=f(X)\) and |\(Y|=\lambda\)] is negligible in \(\lambda\), where X is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and Y is the single output of \(I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function \(\mu :N\to [0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(d\ge 1\) there is \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(\mu (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- d}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in \(\lambda\). They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a \(\lambda\)-bit string \(K_{A},K_{B}\). Correctness requires \(\Pr [K_{A}\ne K_{B}]\) to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let \(U_{\lambda}\) be an independent uniform \(\lambda\)-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher \(D, |\Pr [D(1^{\lambda},T,K_{A})=1]- \Pr [D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]|\) must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and \(U_{\lambda}\). The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Determine whether generic one-wayness is enough to establish a shared classical secret without prior shared randomness or setup.

importance.reason: A foundational boundary between symmetric cryptographic hardness and secret establishment through public interaction. Distinct from the existing stronger PKE-from-OWF target, and supported by a long research line on black-box barriers.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.
